articles.title: Iran is functioning without a supreme leader
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
“Yeki bood, yeki nabood,” Persian stories begin: “There was one, and there was no one.” Just such a fairy tale has taken over political life in Iran. For four decades there was a micromanaging supreme leader. Now there is no one. Mojtaba Khamenei, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s son, is said to have survived the Israeli strike that killed much of his family on the first day of the war. He formally rules in his father’s place. But he has neither been seen nor heard since. Iranians are discovering life without a meddlesome cleric at the helm.

Until the Islamic revolution in 1979, Shiism had been led by a hidden imam for more than a millennium. Today, Iranian officials and Western intelligence agencies insist Mojtaba remains alive. He is said to remain underground because of a reasonable fear of assassination. Some regime hands say he is controlling affairs behind the scenes, but his silence is deafening.

Even if he were active in politics, Mojtaba would need time to consolidate power, given lingering opposition to dynastic succession and his limited religious credentials. In his absence the Islamic Republic’s clerical imprint has grown visibly lighter. Iranians returning from abroad since the war include a pop star sentenced in absentia for incorporating Koranic verses into his songs. Even the daughters of some officials uncover their hair. Some smarter restaurants in Tehran now serve French wine.

The most important shift is in how the regime wields power. “What’s principally changed is that there’s no clear, final arbiter,” says Sanam Vakil of Chatham House, a think-tank in London. Appointments to the state broadcaster, government ministries and the judiciary were once subject to approval by the supreme leader’s 44,000-man court; today the executive has a freer hand. “Israel did Iranians a favour getting rid of Khamenei,” quipped an Iranian academic recently in Tehran. “You don’t need to wait any longer for his legitimation [or approval]. It’s more efficient.”

Instead, six men, all from the ranks of the Supreme National Security Council, a 13-man body of generals and bureaucrats, dominate decision-making. They are believed to include Masoud Pezeshkian, the president; Major General Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran’s principal military force; Mohsen Rezaei, the council’s secretary and a former IRGC chief; Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, the speaker of parliament and a former IRGC brigadier general; Ali Abdollahi, the chief of the general staff of the armed forces; and Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, the only other civilian among them.

The biggest decisions require the collective’s consent. These include matters such as talks about ending or restarting the war with America or nuclear policy. But they each also have a degree of autonomy. Mr Rezaei has been a stalwart of the system since becoming IRGC chief during the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s. Mr Vahidi keeps order in the ranks of the IRGC; and Mr Qalibaf runs parliament’s affairs.

Mr Pezeshkian has largely been left to manage a war-induced depression and a currency in near free fall. The economy was down by 10% in the second quarter of this year compared with the same period in 2025. Unemployment has swelled by half a million since the war began, even as the labour force shrinks and over half of all jobs are now informal. And yet Mr Pezeshkian seems to be managing the fallout from war better than many had expected. He has kept the lights on, despite oil refineries and power plants being bombed.

Mr Pezeshkian has tried to open Iran’s borders to trade since the war began. Overland trade has increased. Some tankers are reportedly paying the tolls Iran demands for passage via the Strait of Hormuz. But Iran is struggling to evade America’s blockade on the export of oil from the southern ports. America’s armada cannot hermetically seal all 2,800km of Iran’s coastline, but estimates of exports in September averaged 260,000 barrels per day, or only around one-sixth of the pre-war flow.

Not all senior officials neatly fit under the six-man committee’s command, however. Domestic control remains largely in the hands of Hossein Taeb, an IRGC hard-man, former intelligence chief and clerical ideologue. He is said to have strong-armed clerics into electing Mojtaba, a longtime confidant, and has long been disliked by some within the establishment for his enthusiasm for a hereditary dynasty. His current role as head of the Basij, a vast paramilitary force, gives him a powerful base.

Since the war began his henchmen and -women have staged nightly rallies in squares across Iran, where anti-regime protesters might otherwise gather. They have distributed rifles to loyalists. In a further effort to intimidate would-be dissidents, Mr Taeb has overseen nearly 700 executions this year. In January the regime crushed nationwide demonstrations with massacres. The war has also helped suppress unrest. Patriotic sentiment has grown as the country’s infrastructure came under American and Israeli attack. Domestic unrest has slipped.

On questions of war and peace, the six-man council has set aside ideological differences. Where the supreme leader once dithered, it moves decisively. The council’s latest diplomatic initiative suggests inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency could return to Iran within two days of America accepting Iran’s proposal. That implies a slightly more flexible position than Iran offered in June. According to one Iranian official, Iran might waive its demand for tolls in Hormuz. And this time, says the official, Iran would not walk away from talks even if Israel continued bombing Lebanon.

Yet the leadership council is also willing to break the deadlock by force. Khamenei senior refrained from disrupting trade through Hormuz; Iran’s new leaders have tolerated its closure for months. In September they set seven “non-negotiable” conditions for ending the stand-off. They have hinted at reviving Iran’s nuclear programme if the blockade continues. “We will not allow even a single particle of enriched nuclear material to leave Iran,” Mr Rezaei said on November 11th. Confrontation with America has also pushed Iran to tighten its ties to Russia and China.

Donald Trump’s Damocles sword, the threat of resuming full-scale war, remains the biggest danger. But Mr Rezaei and his officials have met bombast with bombast and project confidence in their ability to deal with it. “Like for like,” says an official when asked how Iran will respond to attacks on shipping in the Caspian Sea, power infrastructure or its gasfields.

If fighting resumes, Iran’s leaders expect that they would determine its end. The Democrats’ control of Congress may complicate Mr Trump’s freedom to carry out military action. Iran faces no equivalent political deadline. A devolved chain of command would ensure that missiles keep flying even if senior commanders are killed. The regime’s new leaders are counting on outlasting Mr Trump.

articles.title: Bangladesh is no longer a development superstar
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
EKANTTO, THE owner of a café in Dhaka, has not been able to withdraw money from the bank for a year. “Every time I went to the office there were no answers,” he says. He was only told that the bank has a “liquid shortage”—and he is not alone. Depositors at half a dozen institutions have complained they cannot get at funds they had squirrelled away to see their children married or parents buried.

Large parts of Bangladesh’s banking system are on the edge of insolvency. That is partly due to looting under the autocratic regime of Sheikh Hasina Wajed, which held power for 15 years before being toppled by student-led protests in 2024. Corruption has saddled banks with bad loans, many of which will never be paid back. Oligarchs who both ran and borrowed from the banks have been jailed or have absconded. The result is that non-performing loans (NPLs) now make up around a third of the banking sector’s total loan book; in India, by contrast, the share stands at 1.7%; in Pakistan, 5%. As a result, the sector overall is insolvent: capital to risk-weighted assets, a measure of net worth, is a negative 3.8%.

This threatens an unfavourable resolution to the “Bangladesh paradox” of excellent economic outcomes and terrible political ones in the world’s eighth-most populous country, home to 180m people. Officials in America’s State Department described the country as a “basket case” at its independence in 1971: poor, prone to flooding and exporting little to the rest of the world beyond refugees. Yet it became a surprising development success story. It grew rapidly, reduced poverty, and improved health and education. It did so despite poor governance and weak institutions: Bangladesh has pinballed between flawed democracy and military coups.

The newly elected government is struggling to cement its authority. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), the historic rival of Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, replaced a technocratic interim government following elections in February. The BNP now faces a squeeze both from the banking system and strikes in the garment sector , the most important and successful export industry. And it is struggling to maintain order. After Sheikh Hasina said she was planning to return to the country in December, over 50 improvised bombs exploded in the capital; the government says her Awami League is behind them. She is probably bluffing (she has been sentenced to death in absentia for her role in a bloody crackdown), but if she does return she will become a focus for protest.

Banks are where the economy meets Bangladesh’s torrid politics. “The inheritance of the kleptocratic way of plundering the banks, that’s what we are dealing with,” says Debapriya Bhattacharya, who wrote a paper for the interim government on looting during Sheikh Hasina’s regime. Bad loans are concentrated in two kinds of banks (see chart 1): Islamic ones, which follow religious prohibitions on interest, and state-owned ones, controlled by the Ministry of Finance. Cronies of the Awami League were appointed to senior positions in both. The country’s regular commercial banks are doing better.

Take Islami Bank, which is one of the country’s biggest lenders. It had ties to Jamaat-e-Islami, an Islamist opposition party banned under the Awami League, and was forcibly taken over by S Alam, a conglomerate, having been accused of terrorist financing, which it denies. S Alam’s owner, Mohammed Saiful Alam Masud, is an ally of Sheikh Hasina. Around half the bank’s loans subsequently went to S Alam companies. Since Sheikh Hasina was forced from power, Mr Masud, a Singaporean national, has disappeared from view. Jamaat argues the charges against the banks were trumped up to hand the business over to cronies of the Awami League. Mr Masud denies any wrongdoing.

On the positive side, some of the increase in NPLs is thanks to greater transparency. In 2019 the Bangladesh Bank, the central bank, let borrowers repay 2% of the principal of outstanding loans and then defer further payments for a year and gain a decade to pay off the balance. Once the 2% was paid the loans no longer counted as non-performing. In 2020, the IMF warned that the true proportion of NPLs could be up to twice the official figure of about 10%. In 2025, under the interim government, the definition changed to include loans that were 90 days overdue, the international standard. Now the NPL share is at 33%.

Yet the banking crisis risks squashing development. Private-credit growth has fallen from around 10% in 2025 to 4.5% this year, the lowest in 33 years. Growth is forecast to be only 3.7% this year (see chart 2), down from the 6.5% typical before Sheikh Hasina’s fall. The slowdown is not solely due to financial problems. Energy shortages in the early months of the war in the Gulf led to factory closures. Now production is hampered by strikes. The World Bank thinks the poverty rate will grow for the third year in a row in 2026, a reversal of decades of decline. So far the central bank has pumped $6.2bn (1.2% of GDP) of emergency support into the banks. That is nowhere near enough. Moody’s, a rating agency, estimates the sector needs recapitalisation worth 10% of GDP.

There are also worrying signs that the new government is dragging its feet. In June it introduced interest rescheduling for some distressed borrowers. Another new rule limits how much banks can charge in interest, preventing lenders from properly pricing risk. “We are not kicking the can down the road,” says Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, the finance minister. “We are trying to clean up the balance-sheet. And if there is a good asset which needs support, which can be extended a little bit, [we will] be able to give them space to pay it back.”

In the absence of substantial support from abroad, the government has few resources with which to recapitalise the banks. Tax receipts are low, because of widespread avoidance. The government collects just 7% of GDP as revenue. That is a pittance even for South Asia; Pakistan collects around 10%. The government is also running a deficit of 3.3% of GDP, partly to fund subsidies for food and fuel, meaning it is dependent on banks (mainly private, well-capitalised ones) for finance. That, as well as the central bank’s emergency liquidity support, is pushing up the money supply and fuelling inflation.

Bangladesh’s stagflating economy can no longer sail on separately from its politics. One economist suggests that oligarchs linked to the BNP have been waiting for 15 years for their turn to loot. That may give them a reason to clean up the banks, and offer a route to reward a new set of cronies. As a former official puts it: “Fundamentally, nothing has changed.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s giant IPO puts the heat on OpenAI
articles.author: The Economist
articles.body_markdown:
You could forgive OpenAI’s bosses for feeling miffed. Their release of ChatGPT four years ago set the artificial-intelligence boom in motion. Before long countless chatbot imitators had emerged, but none has caught up in popularity. By last year OpenAI’s annual revenue had reached $13bn—then nearly triple that of its arch-rival, Anthropic (see chart).

And yet it is Anthropic, founded by OpenAI secessionists, that has raised the largest sum of all time through an initial public offering (IPO), with a total haul of $107bn. Before trading began on November 19th, after we went to press, the firm was worth $1.5trn, topping the $1.3trn at which the still unlisted OpenAI was valued in a recent private fundraising round.

OpenAI may have led the first phase of competition among model-makers, based around chatbots, but Anthropic trounced it in the second, where coding agents became the biggest source of business. Usage of Claude Code, Anthropic’s software-writing bot, has rocketed this year. As a result, Goldman Sachs, the lead investment bank on the AI company’s IPO, expects it to pull in $53bn of revenue in 2026, more than ten times the figure of a year before and comfortably ahead of OpenAI, which expects $35bn (though direct comparisons are tricky, as Anthropic registers all sales through cloud partners as revenue, whereas OpenAI strips out the share it pays to them).

Still, the past few years show how quickly leads can be lost in the fast-evolving AI market. Use of OpenAI’s own programming tool, Codex, has grown rapidly in recent months. More important, with both model-makers hunting for their next big source of revenue, a new phase in the competition looks set to begin. Anthropic and OpenAI are eagerly pushing to expand the use of agents into all corners of knowledge work. But OpenAI is also betting on a number of other means of monetising its technology. Which strategy will win?

Both firms are counting on blistering growth in the years ahead to justify their valuations. Goldman Sachs projects that Anthropic’s annual revenue will hit $636bn in 2030; William Blair, an investment bank not working on the IPO, forecasts $414bn. OpenAI, for its part, recently told investors it was shooting for $446bn in 2030.

Having lost ground to its main rival, OpenAI has lately been picking up the pace. Last week it told investors that revenue from its enterprise sales doubled in the third quarter compared with the preceding three months, helped by price discounts intended to undercut Anthropic.

For the pair, however, enterprise spending remains concentrated. Revenue from agents currently adheres to an “extreme power law”, says one Anthropic investor. The biggest customers contribute an unusually high share of sales, and the heaviest users within those companies—who are nearly always software engineers—are behind much of the spending.

That poses a risk if these users switch to cheaper models, as many have begun to do. But it also suggests that there is still plenty of scope to extend adoption. This year Anthropic and OpenAI have both rolled out general-purpose enterprise agents that non-coders can use to perform a wide variety of tasks. And in addition to working with the consulting giants, the model-makers have set up their own independent advisory businesses, with private-equity backing, to help customers deploy their technology. A person familiar with Anthropic’s Ode, which is supported by Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman, says that more than half of the clients it has helped to redesign their processes have boosted their profits by at least $10m. Last month Anthropic established a separate consulting venture with Hg, another private-equity firm, focused on Europe.

Aaron Levie, chief executive of Box, a cloud-storage company that works with both AI labs, says that having “the right kind of product experiences with the right sales efforts” could prove even more important than having the best models. Even so, the models will still matter—and here Anthropic holds a clear lead. Investors in both firms reckon performance on “long-horizon” tasks that take several hours or even days—such as building an app from scratch—will become increasingly important for the frontier labs as businesses make greater use of less capable models for simpler work to keep costs down. On MirrorCode, one long-horizon benchmark, OpenAI’s leading model, released last month, is still outperformed by the top offering from Anthropic as far back as July.

That may reflect Anthropic’s more specialised research programme. Whereas OpenAI has sought to remain at the frontier across a wide range of capabilities, including image and voice, Anthropic has focused on the ability of its models to write code and interact with other software.

That, in turn, highlights a difference in the strategies of the two. Although OpenAI has sought to regain ground in enterprise applications, the consumer segment remains a priority. ChatGPT has 1.2bn weekly users worldwide, almost 100m of whom pay upwards of $8 a month for a subscription. Even those who don’t pay provide OpenAI with revenue via the advertising business it launched in February, which by August had an annualised revenue of $1bn.

By contrast, Anthropic’s IPO prospectus barely mentions consumers. It has sworn off advertising, worrying it could muddy Claude’s ability to give helpful answers and incentivise the company to build addictive products.

That leaves OpenAI with a bigger addressable market. But its approach has drawbacks, too. In the consumer segment it must compete with Google, whose Gemini chatbot has gained ground over the past year, as well as personal agents such as Instinct and Meta’s Muse, which have beguiled users with their ability to take on tasks from arranging a dinner with friends to securing sold-out concert tickets.

OpenAI has deprioritised some efforts, shutting down its video-generation tool, Sora, in March. But it continues to pursue a strikingly broad set of opportunities. In the coming year it is expected to unveil a device—a small doughnut-shaped speaker—that consumers can use to interact with its AI systems. It is also developing a humanoid robot. The danger is that it spreads itself too thinly. Unlike Anthropic, which generated its first quarterly operating profit in the second three months of this year, OpenAI remains deep in the red. It will need to follow its rival into the public markets as soon as it can.

OpenAI may have led the first phase of competition among model-makers, based around chatbots, but Anthropic trounced it in the second, where coding agents became the biggest source of business. Still, the past few years show how quickly leads can be lost in the fast-evolving AI market. Use of OpenAI’s own programming tool, Codex, has grown rapidly in recent months. Anthropic and OpenAI are eagerly pushing to expand the use of agents into all corners of knowledge work. But OpenAI is also betting on a number of other means of monetising its technology. Which strategy will win?

Both firms are counting on blistering growth in the years ahead to justify their valuations. articles.title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
articles.author: Robert Faturechi and Aaron C. Davis
articles.body_markdown:
In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.

Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.

Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.

It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which Hadrian specializes in.

In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits and risks.)

At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder, Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-one problem that the Navy’s identified is we can’t find enough skilled workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” he told reporters. The factory will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.

The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”

Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion — more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook.

When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow. A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval vessels.” Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just $6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation.

Hadrian executives told Forbes in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but outside estimates put it at a few hundred.

This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa, Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January. The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years.

A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and funded by Congress, some former defense officials said.

The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense contractors and other private-sector businesses.

But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government.

When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial applications.”

The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on their capital investment.

David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its size.

A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to allow it to continue issuing new loans.

“OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said. “Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that exceed its mandate.”

In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has shown a personal interest in defense tech and has criticized cronyism in defense spending.

The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company.

Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time, Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president, ProPublica previously reported. After defense officials got the White House request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a matter of weeks.

The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played no role in the deal.

articles.title: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
articles.author: Colleen DeGuzman and Rachel Denny Clow
articles.body_markdown:
Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf Coast.

The city would drill wells — lots of them.

Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it threatened their access to water. They mobilized to create a groundwater conservation district that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much water the city could pump.

Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well regulator.

The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors, and its staff is made up entirely of city employees.

Since that decision last fall, the entity — called the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery Conservation District — has greenlit every city request to drill more wells. In doing so, The Texas Tribune and KRIS 6 found, it fast-tracked its permitting process for the city and overlooked steps that would have slowed down the process for approving the permits — safeguards its own rules require to protect other well users.

A city-commissioned study released this summer found that the drilling plan could cause land around the wells to sink and water levels in other nearby wells to drop significantly. But by then, the district had already approved permits allowing the city to pump up to about 40 million gallons a day from 20 wells, although the city draws less than a third of that daily on average.

The city defended the approvals. It said the district’s rules let the board decide when it has enough information to sign off on a permit and that before it does so, the city gives estimates of how pumping could affect water levels.

But water experts warn that the amount the city is allowed to pump in such a small area is exorbitant. “It’s absolutely unfathomable,” said Drew Molly, the former chief operating officer of Corpus Christi’s water department.

Molly, who is now chief water officer at Houston’s water department, said the district’s “lightning speed” approval of the city’s permits will cause ripple effects locally and across the state.

In Texas, fights over limited groundwater supplies will likely intensify as the population booms. Groundwater comes from aquifers and makes up more than half of the state’s water supply.

Aquifers stretch underground across counties and, sometimes, across states. The aquifer Corpus Christi draws from serves dozens of communities along the Gulf of Mexico, including some in Louisiana. Overpumping from aquifers is a key concern in Texas because they need rain and time to refill. As droughts get longer, the state’s water plan shows larger drops in groundwater’s availability compared with other sources.

Groundwater pumping must be approached with caution, experts say. In worst-case scenarios, excessive pumping “can wipe an aquifer out,” said Jarrod Reynolds, a groundwater resource engineer.

“It can be a stopgap, it can be a supplement, but it’s something that’s got to be managed,” Reynolds said.

Corpus Christi’s rapid expansion of groundwater wells offers a critical, if not extreme, example of the challenges presented by a patchwork system for regulating the water that cities, businesses and citizens can extract from the ground.

The coastal city of more than 300,000 residents nearly reached a crisis point earlier this year after persistent drought and years of inaction. It was months away from being unable to meet water demand and faced harsh restrictions to conserve supplies.

Drilling for groundwater became an important fix. So when the possibility of tougher regulation loomed in the wake of the rural residents’ efforts, city officials turned to Corpus Christi’s storage and recovery district, an entity created two decades earlier with the power to approve well permits.

The storage and recovery district is one of nearly 100 such groundwater districts in the state, but it’s the only one with City Council-appointed leaders. Most groundwater districts are led by leaders who are either elected or appointed by county officials — an important distinction since counties are not water suppliers, so there is less concern about any conflict of interest.

Corpus Christi leaders insisted in a written statement that the close ties the city shares with its well regulator will not hamstring efforts to protect the aquifer.

“There is no conflict of interest. City employees involved with the District have no personal or financial interest in permitting decisions,” said Ashley Marion, strategic business manager for the city water department, in the written statement. She added that, “The City and District share an interest in protecting and sustainably managing regional groundwater.”

Marion also said the city tracks water levels and physical conditions at the wells and adjusts pumping rates based on daily data and long-term modeling.

But the arrangement has drawn concern from water experts across the state, an outgoing state lawmaker and at least one of the storage and recovery district’s own board members.

“That’s the fox guarding the henhouse,” said Robert Mace, executive director at Texas State University’s Meadows Center for Water and the Environment, which focuses on water and environmental management policy.

What’s happening in Corpus Christi and the surrounding area raises critical questions about how the state manages its limited groundwater resources and who regulates them.

Denise Villalobos was so concerned about the unusual dynamic in Corpus Christi that she planned to file a bill to abolish the storage and recovery district in the upcoming legislative session. The incoming lawmaker, whose term begins in January, was less certain about her approach when interviewed by the newsrooms, saying she needs to talk with her new constituents first. She said any legislation she supports “must strike the right balance between protecting rural groundwater rights and addressing the urgent water needs of our region.”
